title: The Monsoon Pastures
story:
The rains had come to Vrindavan, and the forest had answered them. Where the ground had been dry and tired there was now green; the trees stood heavy with ripening dates and jambu fruit, and water ran bright in the hollows. For weeks the herd had moved through brown grass and dust; now the wood stirred with new life, and the creatures that lived in it went about their days without fear. The verses call this the best of forests in the rains, and the boys could see why. It was into this washed, shining world that Krishna and his elder brother Balarama led the herd.

The cows went slowly, and for a good reason: their udders were heavy with milk, and every step asked care. The forest seemed pleased to receive them — the trees let fall their honey-sweet blossoms as the herd passed, and the deer and the birds did not start or run, as though the boys and their cattle were simply part of the season. There was nothing to guard against that day, no danger waiting in the green shade — only the rains doing what the rains do.

When a sudden shower broke, the boys did what forest people have always done: they sheltered under a spreading tree or in the mouth of a cave and stood listening to the water on the leaves. When the rain passed and the sun came back out over the wet wood, the whole world smelled of earth and green things, and the sweetness of the fallen blossoms hung in the air.

Then they ate. They had brought the simplest of meals — curd and rice — and they set it out on a flat stone near the water and sat down around it together, on the green grass, with the river at their backs and the cows grazing close by. They had been walking since first light, and the food tasted of the walking, and of being young and hungry in the open air. They ate without hurry, the way people eat when nothing in the world is waiting for them. There was nothing more to the feast than that: the food, the stone, the river, and the company.

When the meal was done they lay back on the grass and watched the herd. The cows stood nearby, chewing their cud with eyes half-closed in contentment, and the boys watched them in the same unhurried way, the way one watches a thing that asks nothing of you. All around them the monsoon showed itself — the shining leaves, the full streams, the fruit bending the branches — and it was, the verses say, a beauty of the rains, one that brings happiness in every season and stays in the memory long after it has gone.

No demon came that day. No fire, no danger, no test. There was only the rain-washed forest, the slow cows, the simple food on a stone, and two brothers resting among their friends as the afternoon wore gently on toward evening. They lay there until the shadows began to lengthen; then the cows turned for home, as herds do, and the boys rose and followed, carrying with them an afternoon they would remember without quite knowing why.
reflection: After the demons and the fires, the story pauses for something that needs no rescue and teaches nothing — a meal of curd and rice on a stone, and the sight of contented cows. It is a reminder that the boy-god's life in Vrindavan was also made of such afternoons, and that joy is itself a kind of worship, needing no occasion.
next_story_tease: But the cowherds had begun to wonder at all the boy had done.
hero_scene: Krishna and the cowherd boys sitting around a flat stone at the water's edge eating curd and rice, with contented cows resting on the green grass nearby and the rain-washed forest shining around them.
